name: Roman chair / hyperextension bench

lead: A Roman chair supports your hips while you bend forward and raise your torso again. It trains the lower-back erectors, glutes and hamstrings, which people use to hold a more upright stance and build a fuller back and posterior chain.

The chain is loaded back extensions, then stronger spinal erectors and glutes, then better posture and muscle. It is common strength equipment; no trials were found that test it for posture or appearance.

paras: Users do bodyweight extensions, add a held plate for more load, or use the rear pad for sit-ups. It usually sits alongside deadlifts, rows and core work, and strength gains build over weeks of regular training.
Specific safety guidance is not given in the sources consulted and no injury-rate studies were found. People with back injuries usually check with a clinician or coach about loaded back extension.

angle.text: Roman chairs load the lower back, glutes and hamstrings, building the muscle that holds you upright and fills out the back. It is widely used strength equipment; appearance-specific research is limited.

lead: A Roman chair, also called a hyperextension bench, is a padded training bench that supports the hips or thighs while the user bends forward and raises the torso again. People use it to build the lower back, glutes and hamstrings, which contribute to a thicker back, a fuller posterior and a stronger-looking upright posture.[1]

In the main exercise, the hyperextension, the user lowers the upper body toward the floor from the hips and returns to a straight-back position. Bodyweight supplies resistance, and a held plate or dumbbell increases the load. Variants include Roman chair sit-ups for the abdominals.[1]

Researchers have measured muscle activation on the bench. In a trial of resistance-trained women, the 45-degree Roman chair back extension activated the gluteus maximus about as much as the Romanian deadlift and activated the biceps femoris more.[2] Other studies have looked at how well it trains the lumbar extensors specifically.[3][4]

paras: The apparatus supports the body during exercises, with pads on which the hips or torso rest while the user moves.[1]

In hyperextensions the lower back is the primary target.[1] In Roman chair sit-ups the user lies with the hips supported on the rear pad and bends backward, lifting the upper body with the abdominals; the hip flexors stabilise the pelvis and may become prime movers if it moves.[1] The name 'Roman chair' is also applied to a wall sit and a squat-like movement that use no apparatus.[1]

In a randomized crossover study of 15 resistance-trained women, the Romanian deadlift and the 45-degree Roman chair back extension activated the gluteus maximus more than a seated machine back extension did. The Roman chair produced higher biceps femoris activation than both other exercises, and erector spinae activation did not differ between the three.[2]

A controlled study of healthy volunteers and people with chronic low back pain examined a Roman chair variant with hips flexed at 40 degrees, describing the exercise as popular for back muscle endurance while noting that it does not exclusively target the back muscles.[4] Setups with the pelvis stabilised differently change which muscles do the work.[3]

A 12-week randomized trial of 15 healthy volunteers had one group train weekly on a 45-degree Roman chair with hand-held plates. Their peak isometric lumbar extension torque did not change significantly compared with a non-training control group, even though their training load increased.[5]

A review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that bench and Roman chair trunk extensions, free-weight exercises and machines without pelvic restraint all activated the lumbar extensors during the exercise, but that training studies suggest they may be less effective at producing chronic lumbar-extensor adaptation than restrained machines.[3] The Roman chair has also been used as a test of trunk muscle endurance in school-based fitness studies.[6]

The bench appears in posture and physique routines because of its association with training the spinal erectors, glutes and hamstrings. Few community threads discuss it directly, so its place in forum culture is not documented in detail here.
